name: The Yerkes–Dodson Law
statement: Performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls — and the peak comes sooner for harder tasks.
statementAccent: up to a point, then falls
meaning: A little pressure sharpens performance; too much degrades it, tracing an inverted-U between arousal and how well you do. The catch, present from the start, is that the optimum depends on the task: difficult, demanding work peaks at a lower level of arousal, while simple, well-learned tasks tolerate — or even keep improving under — much higher arousal.
mechanism: Moderate arousal lifts alertness, motivation, and engagement. Excess arousal narrows attention to a tunnel, loads working memory, and impairs problem-solving — which hurts complex tasks that need broad attention more than it hurts simple ones. That is the intuition behind the task-difficulty tilt of the curve. The causal story, though, is asserted more than demonstrated, and 'arousal' is a later gloss on what was originally just electric-shock intensity.

examples.text: Mild nerves before a test or performance can sharpen focus; overwhelming anxiety impairs recall and reasoning. The felt 'sweet spot' of pressure is the everyday face of the inverted-U.

A simple, repetitive task can be done well, or better, under high arousal, whereas a hard problem-solving task peaks at a lower level. This task-difficulty difference is the part of the original finding most worth keeping — and the part the popular curve usually drops.

The 1908 study itself: Japanese 'dancing mice' learned a black/white discrimination in which one box gave a mild shock. Stronger shocks sped learning up to a point, then slowed it — but this inverted-U appeared clearly in only one of the three experiments, and depended on task difficulty.

variants.name: The inverted-U hypothesis
variants.text: The general, popular form — a smooth bell-shaped arousal-versus-performance curve — usually labelled the 'Yerkes–Dodson law', though it is a later construction that often omits the task-difficulty qualification.

variants.name: Hebb's arousal curve
variants.text: The mid-twentieth-century revival: D.O. Hebb's arousal concept (1955) was mapped onto the 1908 result, generalising it to humans. The textbook graph reproduced everywhere is essentially Hebb's, not a plot of Yerkes and Dodson's data.

whyItMatters: It is the most-cited rule of thumb for the relationship between stress and performance, shaping how coaches, teachers, and managers think about pressure. Its real value is the qualification most people forget — that the optimum shifts with task difficulty — and its cautionary tale is how a narrow animal-learning result became a universal 'law'.

working.text: aim for higher arousal on simple, well-drilled tasks and lower arousal on complex, novel ones — the single most defensible part of the law.

working.lead: Treat it as a heuristic, not a measurement
working.text: there is no clean scale of 'arousal' behind the curve; use it to reason qualitatively, not to predict a precise optimum.
because almost any result can be explained after the fact as 'the task was too easy or too hard', resist using the law to rationalise whatever happened.

limits: The original evidence was thin and narrow: learning in about a dozen mice on a shock-avoidance discrimination, with the inverted-U clear in only one of three experiments. 'Arousal' and 'stress' were never measured — shock intensity was reinterpreted as arousal decades later. Replication is poor: follow-ups in chicks and kittens found no slowing at higher shock, and many human studies find simply 'more stress, worse performance' rather than an inverted-U. The mice-to-human and lab-to-life leaps are contested, and the theory risks unfalsifiability through post-hoc 'the task was too easy/hard' reasoning. The ubiquitous smooth graph is a construction, not the 1908 data.
misreadings: It is not an established quantitative law, and the famous smooth curve is not a plot of Yerkes and Dodson's results — it is a mid-century elaboration built on Hebb's arousal concept. The popular version also drops the original's key point, wrongly implying that too much arousal harms even simple tasks. Treat it as lore with a defensible core, not a measured constant.
origin: From Robert M. Yerkes and John Dillingham Dodson's 1908 paper 'The Relation of Strength of Stimulus to Rapidity of Habit-Formation' (Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology), an animal-learning study in mice. The paper was cited only a handful of times for half a century; interest revived in the 1950s when D.O. Hebb's arousal theory was mapped onto it, producing the human 'arousal versus performance' curve now attached to the name.

sources.text: Yerkes, R.M. & Dodson, J.D. (1908). "The Relation of Strength of Stimulus to Rapidity of Habit-Formation." Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology, 18, 459–482.
Yerkes–Dodson law, Wikipedia. — the inverted-U, the task-difficulty modulation, and the Hebb-era reconstruction.
"Yerkes-Dodson: Lore, not Law," The Learning Scientists (2024). — the gap between the 1908 mouse study and the popular curve.
